figures.caption: Figure 1: Environment Overview. (a) The fly policy is trained in an environment with obstacles and multiple odor sources. (b) The policy is then evaluated in a tethered-ball environment where the fly is head-fixed. The angular and forward velocities are read from the ball, analogous to the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023). (c) The policy receives olfaction as a weighted sum of intensities sampled at the antennae and maxillary palps. (d) The policy’s proprioceptive input comes directly from NeuroMechFly and includes joint angles, joint velocities, and body-frame gravity, height, and linear and angular velocities. (e) Vision is also provided to the policy by simulating the ommatidia mapping of pale and yellow type cells to pixels.

Figure 2: Agent Architecture Overview. (a) The FlyGym simulator provides visual, proprioceptive, and olfactory observations from a biomechanically realistic fly body. Modality-specific CNN and MLP encoders embed these observations into a shared representation ϕt, which is provided to the actor–critic and intrinsic drive module. When applicable, the policy is additionally conditioned on a sampled skill z. The intrinsic drive module computes an intrinsic reward from the encoded state transition and selected action. The actor outputs a categorical distribution over discrete motor primitives, while the critic estimates the state value. The policy selects a new motor primitive every 100 ms. (b) Locomotor primitives are translated into joint-level commands by a low-level central pattern generator (CPG) controller, while grooming is executed using a kinematic replay. These motor commands are applied within the FlyGym physics simulation, which is integrated with a timestep of 100µs. Thus, each policy action is executed for 1,000 physics steps before the next action is selected.

Figure 3: Turn-direction decoding from neural and behavioral data. Prospective coding is quantified as balanced accuracy in predicting future left/right turns. (a,c) Neural (a) and behavioral (c) prospective coding in the fly and models using elastic-net logistic regression in the −15 to −8 s window. (b) Neural and behavioral decoding before (−15 to −8 s) and during (−0.4 to +0.4 s) turns. (d) Behavioral versus neural prospective coding. The dashed line defines the fly’s behavioralto-neural accuracy ratio, which DIAYN closely matches. (e) Models with no turns or only one turn direction, precluding stratified cross-validation.

Figure 4: Turning Bias. (a) Distribution of turning bias across evaluation rollouts for each method. Points indicate individual rollouts, with the mean and range shown for each method. DIAYN produces a broad distribution of turning biases spanning more of the fly-to-fly variability than the other evaluated methods. Methods with a rollout containing no turns or turns in only one direction are excluded because log(NR/NL) is undefined for those rollouts. (b) Virtual x-y trajectories integrated from the ball state of the nine flies and the nine DIAYN evaluation skills drawn from a common origin.

Figure 5: Low-dimensional internal structures relate to ω and v. (a) Reconstructed from Brezovec et al. (2023), the IPS of the fly brain has an interhemispheric relationship of z-scored activity that is correlated with angular (interhemispheric difference) and forward velocity (interhemispheric sum). (b) As a functional analogue of the bilateral supercluster pairs in Brezovec et al. (2023), we use PCA to find principal components in the network activation of the LSTM layer of the Actor in the policy whose difference correlates with angular velocity and whose sum correlates with forward velocity. This structural relationship appears in DIAYN’s Actor LSTM layer (b) but, does not appear in (c) the randomly initialized DIAYN model. (d) We rank each IDM by the mean of the squared Pearson correlations of its angular and forward heatmaps with the fly’s. Higher is a closer match.
Table 1: Seven discrete behavioral primitives. The sign of d sets the stepping direction of that side’s legs (negative is backward) and |d| sets the stepping amplitude.
Table 3: Intrinsic drive methods. Parameter counts exclude frozen targets, lagged copies, and memories.

Table 4: Recorded training time for the IDM-trained policies. Hours sum the final rollout-end timer reading from each process, rounded to 0.1 hour, and are lower bounds on full job time. Decisions/s is 50,176,000 divided by that summed time.
Table 5: PPO training and environment hyperparameters.
Table 6: Turns per fly in the biological dataset.

Table 7: Extended per-method results. Accuracy is balanced accuracy; uncertainty is fold s.d. where shown. † Turning bias averaged over only the indicated number of rollouts; the remaining rollouts turned in only one direction (or not at all), so their bias is undefined. NL and NR are summed over all nine rollouts. ‡ marks a tie at maximum accuracy.

Table 8: Early-window (−15 to −8 s) balanced decoding accuracy for each candidate network feature set and the raw-observation control. A-LSTM and C-LSTM denote the actor and critic LSTM hidden states; Pol and Val denote the policy- and value-MLP hidden representations; Actor concatenates A-LSTM+Pol; Critic concatenates C-LSTM+Val; and All concatenates all five recorded internal representations, including the learned observation embedding. Raw obs. denotes the proprioceptive input with vision and odor set to zero and is distinct from the learned observation embedding. Bold denotes the selected network representation (argmax over the seven network feature sets only).† indicates that the raw-observation control achieved higher decoding accuracy than the selected internal representation. – indicates that decoding was not scored because fewer than two bouts were available in one class.
